summary: This program defines a function that makes Beepo the robot waiter announce its arrival at a given table, then calls that function three times with different table numbers.

lines.text: The `def` keyword defines a new function named `beepo_greet`. The name inside the parentheses is a parameter: a placeholder that stands for whatever table number is supplied when the function is called.

lines.code: """Beepo the robot waiter greets at the specified table."""
lines.text: A string on the first line of a function body is a docstring, the standard way to record in one sentence what the function does for anyone reading or using it later.

lines.code: print(f"Beep boop! Rolling up to table {table_number}...")
lines.text: The `f` before the quotes makes this an f-string, so `{table_number}` is replaced by the value the parameter holds rather than printed literally.

lines.code: print(f"Welcome to table {table_number}! How can I assist you today?")
lines.text: Both print statements are indented, which is how Python knows they belong to the function and should run only when it is called.
Calling the function with the value 1 runs its body with `table_number` set to 1. This is the payoff of a function: one definition, reused as often as you like.
A third call with a different argument produces different output from exactly the same code, which is why functions save you from copying and pasting print statements.
